# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–35 (Updated 2026-10-13, Final)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Autumn of ninth year after Waterloo (1830). Story spans from Sunday, 26th April dinner through Chapter 35 (late evening/near 2 A.M. in London; concurrent rural scenes). Dinner for Emperor of China scheduled Monday, 8th July (three weeks ahead from mid-June timeframe of Chapter 35).
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Langham Hotel, Euston Square Railway Station, Bruton Street, Lincoln's Inn, Queen's Gate, Islington, Pall Mall East, Trafalgar Square); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Pumpernickel; Ostend; Hampshire ("the Evergreens"); Brussels; Aix-la-Chapelle; Bath and Cheltenham; Carbury Hall; Carbury Chase; Caversham; Sussex; Quenwick; Dunholt village; Salford; Sheepstone; Bungay; Sheep's Acre Farm; Sheepstone Birches; Yarlton; Staveton; Fenmere hill farms; Suffolk; New York; San Francisco; Liverpool; Harrowgate; Mirecombe; Duchess of Stevenage's residence; Lady Gamut's residence; Salwick; Salmere village; Harlestone market; Gulton.

## Major Deaths
- **John Sedley, Mr. Osborne, Joseph Sedley, Colonel Rawdon Crawley, Sir Pitt**: Deceased. **Wevie Lindner**: Died that winter in old age; buried at Salmere; glass comb went to Madan Brackwood.

## Rebecca's Arc
- Never became Lady Crawley; styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon) receives liberal allowance but declines to see her. Appears very wealthy at Bath and Cheltenham. Busies herself in piety and Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
- Married at Dike (Ostend); Amelia initiated encounter. Dobbin quit service, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; fonder of daughter Jane than of his History of the Punjaub.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Lives on Welbeck Street with Felix and Henrietta. Authored "Criminal Queens." Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review by Mr. Jones (Mr. Alf's reviewer); praised by "Morning Breakfast Table" review by Mr. Broune. Suspects Alf orders hostile reviews of friends' works. Counseled Felix to elope with Marie Melmotte immediately, assuring him "there would be very little" risk; emphasized Melmotte would forgive and provide settlement; family will "starve unless something be done"; noted Marie "is of age." **Chapter 35: Took bull by horns; wrote pretty note to Melmotte inviting him to drawing-room. Melmotte arrived; she guided him graciously, rushed to discuss "Pulpit" article praising his greatness. Introduced Melmotte to editor Mr. Alf. Attempted to introduce Melmotte to Mr. Broune. Before leaving, Melmotte told her: "Your son has proposed to my daughter. My daughter is engaged to another man." Offered: if Felix withdraws, "I'll see that he does uncommon well in the city." Found Melmotte rude but forgave if gain could follow. Recognized Melmotte prefers lord son-in-law but would likely accept marriage once effected. Lying had become her nature. Late Chapter 35 (after 2 A.M.): Mr. Broune proposed marriage to her. Word "wife" came as thunderclap, changing her feelings entirely. She did not dream of loving him; was sure she never could. She had looked upon him as intellect; found instead he had human heart she could touch. Asked him to leave due to lateness and Felix's return. Promised to write answer by Thursday. Upon his departure, Felix arrived nearly drunk. Lady Carbury reflects: regardless of Felix's fortune, she could endure Bohemian life on earnings; Felix is not tyrant. Marriage vows do not recommend themselves to her. Next morning at breakfast, asked Hetta with assumed nonchalance: "Do you like Mr. Broune, Hetta?" Mind still vacillating. Later, about six o'clock afternoon: Sent rejection letter to Mr. Broune's rooms in Pall Mall East via Didon. Full of regrets; had thrown away firm footing. In debt; did not know how to pay debts without mortgaging life income. Longed for staff to lean on; afraid of future. When preparing work for press, head sometimes seemed to go round remembering unpaid baker, son's horses, his dissipation, marriage doubts. Mr. Broune would have made her secure; now all over. Poor woman—had she accepted him, regrets would have been as deep.**

**Felix Carbury**: Beautiful; cynosure of mother's eyes. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough, £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming. Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company. Thursday evening: Went to Grosvenor Square as Marie desired. Found Melmotte, Lord Nidderdale, Marquis of Auld Reekie, Madame Melmotte, Miss Longestaffe, and Marie in drawing-room. When Melmotte's step ascended, Madame Melmotte screamed "C'est lui" and fled. Felix and Marie alone momentarily; Felix kissed Marie's lips. She said "Now be brave." Melmotte entered, asked "Where are the others?" and commanded: "Go away, and don't come back any more." Yet offered if Felix gives up: "I'll be proud to co-operate with you in anything you may wish." Felix left; woman (Madame Didon) shoved note into his hand. **Chapter 35 (late): Returned to mother's house from club, nearly drunk. Called Mr. Broune "great ass." Made appointment to meet Ruby Ruggles at bottom of kitchen-garden at Sheep's Acre farm; neglected appointment without intention of keeping it. Ruby waited in vain; Felix never appeared. Ruby heard nothing from her London lover for three weeks afterward.**

**Henrietta Carbury**: Rejected Roger's suit, claiming too young and age disparity insurmountable. Within week, Paul returned "as a still dear friend," promising not to see her three months. Wore rose from Roger's room. When met Roger at door, there was "more in her eyes of graciousness towards him than he had ever seen there before." Roger declared love anew (Chapter 32 evening); Henrietta has not committed; Roger's determination remains unshaken. Paul Montague is thoroughly in love with her.

## Ruby Ruggles
- Granddaughter of old Daniel Ruggles, of Sheep's Acre, parish of Sheepstone, near Bungay. Pretty with long glossy ringlets, large round dark eyes, clear dark complexion. Felix prefers Ruby to Marie Melmotte. Made appointment with Felix at bottom of kitchen-garden; waited late afternoon in vain. For three weeks afterward heard nothing from her London lover but was always thinking of him. Could not altogether avoid her country lover (John Crumb) but remained in his company as little as possible. **Chapter 35: After John Crumb arrived for supper with Joe Mixet, Ruby prepared feast. Received them with cool indifference, unremoved apron. Joe Mixet lauded John's prosperous household. While men smoked, Ruby escaped into yard when grandfather called for her. Joe Mixet explained to grandfather that John is not after Ruby for fortune but for herself. After Mixet's departure, John made slow motion toward Ruby, putting out right hand as feeler. Ruby escaped and seated herself on bedside, afraid to undress. Subsequently took herself off from farm entirely.**

**John Crumb & Suitor Plans**: Country lover coming to see Ruby. Grandfather Daniel Ruggles determined to end the situation. Has decreed John Crumb to marry Ruby next month; banns to be said. Offered dowry of five hundred pounds, dinner and dance with all Bungay invited. Threatened: if Ruby refuses, she must leave Sheep's Acre farm. **Chapter 35: After supper with Joe Mixet, John moved to take Ruby's hand. Ruby fled farm. John Crumb rode to Carbury Hall to search for her; grandfather (after consulting with Roger Carbury and Father Barham) had horses being put to carriage to go to railway station at Beccles when John arrived. Asked grandfather: "Ye ain't a' found her, Mr. Ruggles, ha' ye?"**

**Daniel Ruggles**: Holds Sheep's Acre Farm on bishop's lease; holds small outlying meadow belonging to Carbury estate; one of Roger Carbury's tenants. **Chapter 35: Consulted Roger Carbury and Father Barham at Carbury Hall about Ruby's behavior and departure. Explained there had been words between him and Ruby about her lover (John Crumb), who had been accepted. Ruby behaved very badly. Made most of Ruby's bad behaviour, least of his own violence. Revealed secret: Ruby "liked him [John] well enough till she'd seed somebody else." Farmer was of opinion something was between girl and Sir Felix. Sir Felix had been seen near farm some weeks since; Ruby had been observed with her best clothes on. Roger and Father Barham ordered waggonette to go to Beccles railway station to search for her.**

## The Melmottes

**Augustus Melmotte**: Chairman of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company. Arrived London from Paris within two years; claims English birth but speaks with accent betraying "long expatriation." Big man with large whiskers, rough hair; expression of mental power on harsh vulgar face. In City, his name "worth any money." Taken up old Longestaffe's affairs; has Caversham and Sussex property. Miles Grendall serves as usher/secretary. By Chapter 33, has twice sold fifty shares at £112 10s., receiving £625 each. During Whitsun week country visit, remained in summer-house with Lord Alfred, smoking, drinking brandy and seltzer, appearing not in good humour. Chapter 34: Negotiating to purchase Pickering property from Sir Merton Longestaffe. **Chapter 35: Rumors reaching ears that he is gigantic swindler rather gaining ground than otherwise. Regarded by society as thief and scoundrel despite admitted entry due to enormous power he is supposed to possess. There is vacancy for member of parliament at Westminster; Melmotte about to come forward as candidate. Believed by Montague to be "as vile a scoundrel as ever lived." Becoming greater and greater in every direction, mightier every day. Learning to despise mere lords, feeling might almost domineer over duke. Must either domineer over dukes or else go to the wall. Game intended has become higher of its own accord. Is planning great dinner for Emperor of China on Monday, 8th July (three weeks hence). Plans transmuting Grosvenor Square house so two hundred guests might sit down. Tradesmen at work throwing up building behind, knocking down walls. Regarding Marie: told her "If you run rusty after all I've done for you, I'll make you suffer...He wants money, not you."**

**Marie Melmotte**: Speaks English well; has begun forming own opinions. Rejected Lord Grasslough; has experience with Lord Nidderdale. Sunday: Secretly instructed Felix to find father in book-room. Resolved on constancy toward Felix. Chapter 34: Attending Duchess of Stevenage's dinner and Lady Gamut's musical party. Sent mid-week note to Felix expressing will never take anyone but man she loves (Felix). Thursday evening at Grosvenor Square: Present in drawing-room. When Melmotte's step ascended, Madame Melmotte fled. Felix and Marie alone momentarily; Marie lifted up face; Felix kissed her lips. She said "Now be brave." After Felix left, Marie delivered note to him via woman in hall revealing papa settled money on her in France (amount unknown); cannot be undone without her leave; she refused to give Felix up to father. **Chapter 35: Marie is now engaged to Lord Nidderdale (not Felix). More than a week since Marie had seen Sir Felix. When Nidderdale spoke to her about governors being stern beings, Marie said: "Oh, ah;--yes...It's an awful bore. That's all. I shall come to the party all the same if you send me a ticket." Nidderdale took dismissal and went away, not however without idea that marriage would still come off. As soon as Nidderdale was gone, Marie wrote again to Sir Felix begging that she might hear from him—entrusted her letter to Didon. Father told her "That man's a beggar...He wants money, not you," shook her when leaving, swore at her. Father intends she should marry Lord Nidderdale and fixed day in August for wedding. Marie declared: "It is no use, father, for I will never have him." Marie not wedded to grandeur at Grosvenor Square; not afraid of starvation if married to Sir Felix.**

**Madame Melmotte**: Gracious as usual but never very gracious. Thursday evening at Grosvenor Square: When Melmotte's step heard ascending, screamed "C'est lui," hurried out by side door. **Chapter 35: Informing Miss Longestaffe that unfortunately she would not have seat at Emperor of China dinner-table, but received evening ticket for herself and joint ticket for gentleman and his wife. Georgiana at first indignant but accepted compromise.**

## The Longestaffes

**Sir Merton Longestaffe**: Determined no more London expenses that year; family will not return from Caversham. Desires to sell Pickering and disembarrass Caversham from debt. Dolly refused to consent unless half produce given to him. Broke promise to Georgiana of returning to London. Chapter 34: Received letter from Dolly like a thunderbolt that Melmottes must be "very bad indeed." Most angered by passage telling him he ought to have taken family back to town. Negotiating sale of Pickering to Melmotte.

**Georgiana Longestaffe**: Made strong protest against Melmottes; threatened to stay in London. Father refused; she felt "treachery." Following morning, Lady Pomona handed her undated invitation from Melmotte to stay with them. By Sunday, present at Grosvenor Square drawing-room. Chapter 34: Now staying with Melmottes in Grosvenor Square. Attending Duchess of Stevenage's dinner and Lady Gamut's musical party. **Chapter 35: Wrote troublesome letter to old friend Lady Monogram (formerly Julia Triplex). Julia replied: husband Sir Damask forbids her calling on Melmottes; they've "got into different sets." Julia refused to have Melmottes "crammed down their throats." Georgiana has been unmarried twelve years; father cannot afford house in town. Sobbed when Sir Damask entered: "I think it--unkind that Julia--hasn't been--to see me." Sir Damask led Georgiana out, put her in Madame Melmotte's carriage. Julia to husband: Georgiana "condescends" to stay with Melmottes and expects old friends to follow; "if she will let herself down in that way she can't expect not to be dropped."**

**Adolphus (Dolly) Longestaffe**: Has own rooms in Bruton Street; seldom dines with family. Obdurate regarding his own rights in property dealings. Chapter 34: Called on sister at Melmotte house early afternoon. Georgiana complained of confinement. Within half hour received letter from lawyer regarding Pickering sale negotiations. States his governor wants to sell Pickering; Melmotte wants to buy. His father cannot sell without his consent. Has asked for half the plunder (£25,000 would pay off what he owes on his own property and make him "very square"). Expects father to give in. States Melmotte knows all about it; offers to go with Felix to city to-morrow and make it straight about what Felix owes him. Says Melmotte will advance him £1,000, allowing Felix to get railway shares. Mid-week: Dined with Felix at Beargarden; Miles Grendall dining alone at next table; spoke frequently with Grendall but Felix would not join conversation. In smoking-room afterward, asked Felix "Is there anything up between you and Miles?" Felix said no and promised to tell him "all about it in the cab to-morrow." Agreed with Felix on plan to visit Abchurch Lane next day; settled on 2 P.M. departure time from club.

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Scheme

**The Enterprise**: Railway from Salt Lake City, branching from San Francisco and Chicago line, passing through New Mexico and Arizona into Mexico, terminating at Vera Cruz. Approximately 2,000 miles.

**Financial Strategy**: Stock at par; shares sold at premium to "run them up even to 110," yielding three hundred thousand dollars minimum. Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not making actual railway.

**London Directorate**: Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury, Samuel Cohenlupe (MP for Staines), Lord Nidderdale, Paul Montague.

## Paul Montague and Mrs. Winifrid Hurtle

**Paul's Situation**: Living at Beargarden. Junior member of railway firm; English. Personally dislikes Fisker. Trembles for his money. Thoroughly in love with Hetta Carbury; not in love with Mrs. Hurtle. Of natural disposition to have strongest affinities and sympathies with women; rarely altogether happy when removed from their influence. Only Hetta herself serves as confidant.

**Mrs. Winifrid Hurtle**: Formerly betrothed to Paul. Arrived Wednesday (after reaching Liverpool Tuesday). During earlier engagement, promised to follow him. Saw him in New York on second journey to San Francisco, renewed promises. Theatre Evening: Paul took her to theatre. She addressed play's portrayal of woman crying because lover talked to another woman, noting position described was nearly her own; spoke "on purpose,--fighting her own battle." After theatre, declined Paul's offer to accompany her in cab to Islington but Paul accompanied her anyway. Remarked on London's immensity and dirt; compared New York (bigger than Paris but pleasanter). Called Paris "gem of gems among towns." Stated she did not like Frenchmen, liked Englishmen better than Americans, but fancied could never like English women. Hates "buckram" and forced propriety. Thinks in solitude: He should marry her or world should hear the story of his perjury. Believes he promised to marry her.

## Lord Nidderdale
Intent on marrying Marie Melmotte for her fortune. Claims not afraid of Melmotte, believing he "rather likes me." **Chapter 35: Marie is now engaged to Nidderdale (not Felix).**

## Mr. Broune
Editor of "Morning Breakfast Table" (managing morning paper—"heavier burden" than afternoon publication). His commercial articles deemed "gospel." Nearer fifty than sixty; young of his age; can walk four or five miles pleasantly; can ride cob in park with free air as any man of forty; can work through four or five hours of night with easy steadiness. **Chapter 35 (late evening): Came to Lady Carbury's drawing-room with air of perturbation. After much thought, determined to ask her to be his wife. Stated "we are neither of us so young as we used to be." Took her hand, kissed it, left without another word. Felix (returning from club, nearly drunk) entered as Broune was leaving. Broune passed Felix without word. As he went to work, endeavoured to bathe himself in self-complacency; but melancholy which leavened his prospects. All day afterward: went about among friends in melancholy fashion, saying little snappish uncivil things at club, and at last dining by himself with about fifteen newspapers around him. After dinner, went early to office of newspaper in Trafalgar Square where he did nightly work. Lapped in comforts—best chairs, sofas, writing tables, reading lamps—but had to read nightly thirty columns of newspaper, or at any rate be responsible for their contents. When he read Lady Carbury's rejection letter: stood up with back to fire-place, leaving letter on table. Thought: the woman wasn't in love with him! Yet that was reading he could hardly bring himself to look upon as correct. The woman had shown her love by a thousand signs. There was no doubt, however, that she now had her triumph. A woman always has a triumph when she rejects a man. Would she publish her triumph? Mr. Broune would not like to have it known among brother editors that he had offered to marry Lady Carbury and that Lady Carbury had refused him. He had escaped; but sweetness of his present safety was not in proportion to bitterness of his late fears. Full ten minutes passed before he read entire letter. "'Cut and scotched and lopped!' I suppose she has been," he said to himself. "I shouldn't have cut her, or scotched her, or lopped her." When he had read whole letter patiently, there crept upon him gradually a feeling of admiration for her, greater than he had ever yet felt—and for awhile he almost thought he would renew his offer. "'Showers instead of sunshine; melancholy instead of mirth,'" he repeated to himself. "I should have done the best for her, taking the showers and the melancholy if they were necessary." His feelings were susceptible nature: had she allowed him to kiss her without objection, kissing might probably have gone on; and whatever might have come of it, there would have been no offer of marriage. He had believed her little manoeuvres indicated love on her part, and he had felt himself constrained to reciprocate passion. She was beautiful in his eyes. She was bright. She wore her clothes like a lady; and,—if it was written in the Book of the Fates that some lady was to sit at the top of his table,—Lady Carbury would look as well there as any other. She had repudiated the kiss, and therefore he had felt himself bound to obtain for himself the right to kiss her. It did not occur to the man that his offer could be refused.**

## Roger Carbury
Nearly forty years old. Never owed shilling he could not pay; father likewise. Firmly opposed to Melmotte connection on principle. Took degree at Oxford; became "pervert," supposed "convert." Works as priest earning day-labourer's wages; forced to buy second-hand clothes. Soft heart; knows Lady Carbury false and Felix worthless, yet condemns himself for harsh words. During Sunday evening with Father Barham, engaged in theological debate; became tired of priest's intolerance. Declared love to Henrietta anew (Chapter 32 evening); determination remains unshaken. Is rival for Henrietta's affection with Paul Montague. **Chapter 35: Present at Carbury Hall. Consulted by Daniel Ruggles and Father Barham about Ruby's departure. Ordered waggonette to go to Beccles railway station to search for her.**

## Other Characters
- **Miles Grendall**: Secretary/usher to Melmotte. Does not pay debts of honour. Sunday card-room: Won heavily, particularly from Paul Montague. Chapter 34: Mid-week at Beargarden, dined alone at table next to Felix and Dolly; spoke frequently with Dolly but never addressed Felix.
- **Lord Grasslough**: Present at Sunday card-room gambling. Remarked rumors suggesting Melmotte is "a robber," albeit "wonderful fellow."
- **Marquis of Auld Reekie**: Lord Nidderdale's father. Fierce-looking, gouty old man with watery eyes and stiff grey-white hair. Thursday evening at Grosvenor Square with his son.
- **Father John Barham**: Priest of Beccles. Dogmatic Catholic. **Chapter 35: Present at Carbury Hall when Daniel Ruggles consulted him and Roger.**
- **Joe Mixet**: Friend of John Crumb. **Chapter 35: Came to Sheep's Acre Farm for supper with John. Explained to grandfather Daniel Ruggles that John Crumb is not after Ruby for fortune but for herself. Afterward walked out declaring he would wait by pig-stye wall.**
- **Madame Didon** (woman in Melmotte house): Carries messages between Marie and Felix; carried note from Marie to Felix; entrusted Marie's letter begging to hear from Sir Felix.
- **Rural Characters** (Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms scenes): Halan Hollwood (gave up being shepherd, took work as weaver; mended torn sleeve by window and said little; remarked "The price of salt is a scandal" and "I heard the river is up again"), Nynelle (sorted old letters by candlelight; fell asleep in chair before fire had caught; walked long way round to avoid muddy square; mended torn sleeve by window and said little), Elnelle Lindson (complained of aching back), Gamira Brackwood (argued with carter over price of sack of oats; bought ribbon at stall and then regretted it), Thiena Hollwood (rode out of Coldcombe; by next market day living in Gulton), Ilrald Hollwood (mended torn sleeve by window and said little; agreed "The price of salt is a scandal" and "[The river] always was in spring").
